title: The Feasibility of a Hardwired Pause of Frontier AI Training

report.summary: A multidisciplinary paper examines whether frontier AI training could be stopped by technically enforced, verifiable hardware or infrastructure controls rather than voluntary pledges.
report.background: Frontier AI training runs are increasingly concentrated among a few labs, cloud providers, and chip supply chains, prompting debate over whether voluntary safety commitments are sufficient. Interest in compute governance, export controls, training-run monitoring, and emergency pause mechanisms has grown alongside warnings about advanced model risks. A 'hardwired pause' would embed enforcement in hardware, firmware, cloud platforms, or training infrastructure so that a halt is not merely a corporate promise. The listed authors span UC Berkeley, Stanford, Princeton, Tufts, MIT, Mila, and policy/security institutions, covering statistics, philosophy, computer science, economics, political science, international security, and diplomacy. The paper's framing suggests it assesses technical and institutional feasibility, trade-offs, and verification challenges rather than assuming a global kill switch is readily achievable.
key_points: The paper is a multi-disciplinary feasibility assessment, not a single-discipline technical proposal. Its organizers and members span statistics, philosophy, computer science, economics, political science, international security, and diplomacy. That mix signals the core question is not only whether a kill switch can be built, but whether it can be governed, verified, and accepted across jurisdictions.

A 'hardwired pause' would target frontier training runs—the large compute-intensive processes that produce advanced models—rather than ordinary inference or open-source experimentation. Enforcement could sit in chips, firmware, cloud platforms, or training clusters. The appeal is moving beyond voluntary corporate pledges to controls that are harder to reverse, but each layer creates new attack surfaces and compliance questions.

Technical feasibility depends on verification and tamper resistance. A credible pause requires detecting prohibited training, proving a run has stopped, preventing workarounds via other hardware or jurisdictions, and protecting legitimate research. The paper's expert roster suggests it weighs hardware security, statistical detection, supply-chain controls, and international monitoring against false positives and evasion.

Governance design is central: who can trigger a pause, under what threshold, for how long, with what exceptions and appeals? A hardwired mechanism could concentrate power in chipmakers, cloud providers, or states. The paper likely examines treaty-like coordination, export controls, emergency safeguards, and risks of unilateral use or geopolitical retaliation.

The authors' disclaimer—co-authorship does not imply agreement or institutional endorsement—indicates the paper maps trade-offs and feasibility conditions rather than advocating an immediate pause. It may conclude that partial hardwired controls are more plausible than a global switch, and that technical enforcement must be paired with legitimacy, transparency, and international institutions.
report.impact: If credible, a hardwired pause would shift AI safety from voluntary commitments to enforceable infrastructure governance. Frontier labs and cloud providers would face verification, audit, and compliance costs; chip and cloud providers become regulatory chokepoints. Developers may see stricter access to large compute, training-run registration, and security requirements, while small and open-source work could face collateral friction. Regular users might not notice short-term changes, but model releases and service availability could become more conditioned on safety triggers. The bigger impact is precedent: treating frontier training as a globally monitorable activity, with sovereignty, innovation, and civil-liberties trade-offs similar to other dual-use technologies.
report.tools: For follow-up, read the paper at hardwired-pause.ai and track work from the Berkeley Risk and Security Lab, Center for AI Safety, and GovAI on compute governance. Technical readers can examine open-source hardware root-of-trust projects such as OpenTitan, confidential-computing primitives, and training-run logging or verification tools; policy readers can watch AI incident databases and compute-threshold/export-control trackers. These are not plug-and-play pause mechanisms, but they illustrate the enforcement and verification stack a hardwired pause would need.
